item.title: Mini Payments: a volume for Postgres
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: 10 November: a 5Gi ReadWriteOnce PersistentVolumeClaim at /var/lib/postgresql/data. The database is still a Deployment, not a StatefulSet.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
The same day as the ConfigMap, after that fight, I gave Postgres a disk. The commit is “PVC/PV fixed for database”.
k8s/database-pvc.yaml:
apiVersion:v1kind:PersistentVolumeClaimmetadata:name:database-pvcspec:resources:requests:storage:5GivolumeMode:FilesystemaccessModes:-ReadWriteOnce
The database Deployment mounts that claim at/var/lib/postgresql/data:
volumeMounts:-name:database-storagemountPath:/var/lib/postgresql/datavolumes:-name:database-storagepersistentVolumeClaim:claimName:database-pvc
The object is still a Deployment,replicas: 1. A PersistentVolumeClaim is a request for storage. It is not a StatefulSet. A StatefulSet is the controller that gives a stateful app a stable pod name and its own volume per pod. I do not have one.
On this commit I also addedk8s/app-secret.yaml to.gitignore.
What I’m learning next
Planned, not built.
StatefulSet. Stable pod name, own volume per pod. The claim above does not turn this Deployment into one, and raising the replica count still would not.
Liveness and readiness probes. Periodic checks. Readiness decides whether the pod receives traffic. Liveness decides whether it is restarted.
Resource requests and limits. A request is what the scheduler reserves. A limit is the cap. Without a limit, one pod can use up the node. Without a request, the scheduler cannot place it properly.
Ingress. An HTTP router for the cluster, instead ofkubectl port-forward. A LoadBalancer or NodePort service per app does not scale.
CI/CD. Build the image and deploy it, first to the homelab cluster, then to AKS.
Prometheus and Grafana. Actuator with Micrometer collects HTTP requests, memory, threads and database connections. A dependency inpom.xml turns that into Prometheus text format, and the metrics endpoint has to be exposed. Grafana would be the dashboards. I test each step withkubectl describe,kubectl logs andkubectl get events. ]]>

item.title: Mini Payments: build log
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: Index of the Mini Payments build log, from the 15 October plan to a Postgres volume on Minikube.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
I’m buildingMini Payments to practise the path a service takes: code, container, cluster. It’s a small payments API in Java 21 with Spring Boot and PostgreSQL. It has accounts, transfers between them, and business-rule errors when a transfer isn’t allowed.
I scaffolded the Java backend and the small frontend with Claude. My own work is the database, the containers and the Kubernetes setup. The commits below are onfeature/mini-payments-api-skeleton. It runs on Minikube on my machine. A homelab deploy and AKS are still plans.
The posts
15 Oct — Kickoff. The README states the plan.
24 Oct — App and PostgreSQL. The payments role was missing.
25 Oct — Images, Compose, database manifests. 825 MB disk down to 402 MB.
26 Oct — Docker Desktop Kubernetes. Three app replicas, one database replica.
3 Nov — Minikube. The cluster could not see the host image.
9–10 Nov — ConfigMap and Secret. One Secret, two expected key names.
10 Nov — A volume for Postgres. A PersistentVolumeClaim on a Deployment.
Where it stands
The app Deployment has 3 replicas ofmini-payments-api:dev. Postgres 17 is one replica, still a Deployment, with a 5Gi ReadWriteOnce claim mounted at/var/lib/postgresql/data. The database URL and username come from a ConfigMap. The password comes from a Secret. I reach the API withkubectl port-forward.
What I’m learning next
Planned, not built. These are the notes I wrote for the steps after the volume.
StatefulSet. A StatefulSet is the controller for a stateful app: a stable pod name, and its own volume per pod. The volume I have does not make the database Deployment a StatefulSet. Raisingreplicas is not how you make Postgres reliable.
Liveness and readiness probes. Kubernetes checks the container on a schedule. Readiness decides whether traffic may go to the pod. Liveness decides whether the pod should be restarted.
Resource requests and limits. A request is what the scheduler reserves. A limit is the cap on the machine. Without a limit, one pod can use up the node. Without a request, the scheduler cannot place the pod properly.
Ingress. An HTTP router into the cluster, in place of port-forward. A LoadBalancer or NodePort service per app does not scale. Ingress is the one front door.
CI/CD. A pipeline that builds the image and deploys it, first to my homelab cluster, then to AKS.
Prometheus and Grafana. Spring Boot Actuator, with the Micrometer that is already there, collects HTTP requests, memory, threads and database connections. A dependency inpom.xml turns those metrics into the text format Prometheus reads. The endpoint still has to be opened: Spring Boot only exposes health over HTTP until then. Grafana is the dashboard in front of that. I check each of these steps withkubectl describe,kubectl logs andkubectl get events. ]]>

item.title: Mini Payments: the API on Docker Desktop Kubernetes
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: 26 October: the app Deployment at 3 replicas and a Service, on Docker Desktop. Postgres cut from 3 replicas to 1.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
On 26 October I added the app manifests and ran them on the Kubernetes cluster built into Docker Desktop.
k8s/app-deployment.yaml runs 3 replicas ofmini-payments-api:dev. The container listens on 8080. The datasource URL, username and password are environment variables on the pod. The URL isjdbc:postgresql://database:5432/payments and the username ispayments. The password is set the same way. I’m not printing the value.
k8s/app-service.yaml is namedapp. It selects those pods and exposes port 8080. Traffic to the Service is spread across the three replicas.
One database replica
The database Deployment from 25 October asked for 3 replicas. I set it to 1.
Postgres here has no shared disk. Each pod has its own data directory. The Service spreads requests across the pods: the app creates an account through one pod, reads it through another, and gets “not found”. A database is stateful. Adding replicas does not make it reliable. That takes a stable identity per pod and a volume per pod, which is a StatefulSet and a PersistentVolumeClaim. On 26 October I have neither, so the database stays at one replica.
Reaching it
The Services are only inside the cluster. From the laptop:
kubectl port-forward svc/app 8080:8080
To look at the tables, exec into the Postgres pod. The pod I used that day:
kubectlexec -it database-79d5d77c8b-d8lv9 -- psql -U payments -d payments]]>

item.title: Mini Payments: app and PostgreSQL
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: 24 October: Claude scaffolded the Java and the frontend. PostgreSQL 17 is my work, including the missing payments role.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
The commit on 24 October is the base build. The message on it is blunt: the backend and the frontend were built by Claude, and I made the PostgreSQL database myself. That split is the point. I am practising the platform side.
The API is Java 21 and Spring Boot. It has accounts, transfers between them, and business-rule errors when a transfer is not allowed. Flyway appliesV1__create_accounts_and_transfers.sql, so the schema is built the same way every time. The database is PostgreSQL 17.
./mvnw test runs the tests../mvnw spring-boot:run starts the app, and it will not stay up without the database.
The payments role
The first database container did not create thepayments role, so Postgres never became usable and Spring Boot, which waits on it, did not start either. I had passedPOSTGRES_USERS instead ofPOSTGRES_USER. The image does not invent that role. It creates the role fromPOSTGRES_USER.
I removed the container and created it again withPOSTGRES_USER,POSTGRES_PASSWORD andPOSTGRES_DB set, plus a named volume (payments-data mounted at/var/lib/postgresql/data) so the data survives a restart. I’m not putting the password in this post. The database name and the role are bothpayments.
From the host, with the app in a second terminal:
SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/payments\SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME=payments\./mvnw spring-boot:run
And into the database:
psql -h localhost -U payments -d payments
The commands I actually use inpsql:
CommandWhat it does
\conninfoWhich database and user am I connected as?
\dtList the tables
\d accountsColumns, constraints and indexes of a table
\diList the indexes
\xToggle expanded rows
\qQuit
When the app fails to start, check the dependency it is waiting on before debugging the app. ]]>

item.title: Mini Payments: kickoff
item.author: emmanueltekle@gmail.com (Emmanuel Tekle)
item.description: 15 October: the repo and the README plan. A Spring Boot API, PostgreSQL, a Dockerfile, then CI/CD to the homelab.
item.content:encoded:
<![CDATA[
On 15 October I createdmini-payments-api. The README is the plan, written as preparation for an internship.
The plan is a payments API on Java and Spring Boot, a PostgreSQL database, a Dockerfile, and a CI/CD pipeline that deploys to my own Kubernetes cluster on the homelab. Monitoring would be Prometheus and Grafana.
That is the plan. The pipeline, the deploy onto the homelab cluster, and the monitoring are still plans. The posts after this one are the parts that are built. ]]>
